positions/monothelitism/oneLine: Christ has two natures but one ‘theandric’ (divine-human) energy, or one will, since a single person can have only one will.
positions/monothelitism/coreClaims/0: Will belongs to the person, not the nature: one person, one will.
positions/monothelitism/coreClaims/1: Two wills in Christ would imply conflict between them and two subjects.
positions/monothelitism/coreClaims/2: Christ's humanity acts as the instrument of the one divine-human operation.
positions/monothelitism/coreClaims/3: This formula could reconcile Chalcedonians and Miaphysites without abandoning Chalcedon.
positions/monothelitism/origin: Proposed by Patriarch Sergius of Constantinople with Emperor Heraclius (c. 619–633) to reunite Miaphysite provinces against Persia and then the Arabs; the Pact of Union at Alexandria (633), the Ekthesis (638) and later the Typos (648) forbidding discussion. Pope Honorius I endorsed ‘one will’. Condemned by the Lateran Synod (649) and Constantinople III (681).
positions/monothelitism/proponentsOther/: the Maronites (historically associated; they deny holding it)
positions/monothelitism/strongestArgumen: A single person naturally has a single will; two wills seem to divide Christ.
It avoided any hint of internal conflict in Christ's moral life.
Ecumenically, it offered a realistic bridge to Miaphysite Christians at a time of existential threat to the empire.
positions/monothelitism/strongestObjecti: Maximus: will belongs to nature; if Christ has no human will, his humanity is incomplete and our will is not healed (‘the unassumed is unhealed’).
Gethsemane (Matthew 26:39) shows a human will submitting to the divine.
Two wills need not conflict: the human freely follows the divine (Constantinople III).
positions/monothelitism/responses/0: Monothelites argued that the prayer in Gethsemane was an economy for our instruction, not evidence of a separate will.
positions/monothelitism/responses/1: They understood ‘one will’ as a moral unity, not denial of human volition.
positions/monothelitism/consequences/0: The persecution of Pope Martin I (d. 655 in exile) and Maximus the Confessor (d. 662).
positions/monothelitism/consequences/1: The posthumous condemnation of Pope Honorius I (681), later cited in debates on papal infallibility (1870).
positions/monothelitism/consequences/2: Completed the Chalcedonian Christology of two wills and two energies, important for later theology of human freedom and synergy.
positions/kenotic-christology/oneLine: In becoming man the eternal Son ‘emptied himself’ (Philippians 2:7) by laying aside or restricting the exercise of divine attributes such as omniscience and omnipresence, so as to live a truly human life.
positions/kenotic-christology/coreClaims: The incarnation involved real divine self-limitation, not merely a veiling.
Christ's human ignorance (Mark 13:32), growth and dependence on the Spirit are real.
‘Relative’ attributes (omniscience, omnipotence, omnipresence) can be given up while ‘essential’ attributes (love, holiness) remain (Thomasius).
God's power is supremely revealed in self-giving love.
positions/kenotic-christology/origin: Anticipated in 17th-century Lutheran debates (Giessen vs Tübingen, 1619–27) over Christ's use of divine attributes; formulated by Gottfried Thomasius (Christi Person und Werk, 1853) and others at Erlangen; developed in Britain by Charles Gore (Lux Mundi, 1889; Bampton Lectures 1891), H. R. Mackintosh and P. T. Forsyth; revived by some analytic philosophers (Stephen Evans) and evangelicals.
positions/kenotic-christology/strongestA: It takes Philippians 2:7 and the Gospels' portrait of human limitation seriously.
It reconciles orthodox Christology with the results of historical study (Jesus as a first-century Jew with human knowledge).
It presents the incarnation as a costly act of divine love.
positions/kenotic-christology/strongestO: If the Son gives up divine attributes, he ceases to be fully God during the incarnation (‘a depotentiated God’).
What happened to the Son's cosmic functions (upholding all things, Hebrews 1:3) while he was an infant?
Classical Christology (Cyril, Aquinas, Calvin's extra Calvinisticum) explains limitation by the two natures without divine change.
‘Emptied himself’ in Greek idiom may mean ‘made himself nothing’ by taking the form of a servant, not subtracting attributes.
positions/kenotic-christology/responses/: Kenoticists distinguish possession of attributes from their exercise, keeping the Son fully divine.
Some modern forms (Spirit Christology) locate Christ's miracles and knowledge in the Spirit's empowerment rather than in his divine nature.
positions/kenotic-christology/consequenc: Became a way for Anglican and Lutheran theologians to accept biblical criticism while confessing Christ's deity.
Influential in popular evangelical and Pentecostal preaching that Jesus lived ‘as a man filled with the Spirit’.
Some contemporary forms are criticised as quasi-kenotic or ‘functional kenoticism’.
positions/christology-from-below/name: Christology from below (liberal and historical Christology)
positions/christology-from-below/oneLine: Christology should begin with the historical, human Jesus and his unique God-consciousness or relationship to God, rather than with the pre-existent Word and the metaphysics of natures.
positions/christology-from-below/coreCla: The starting point is the Jesus of history and the church's experience of redemption.
Christ's divinity consists in the constant potency of his God-consciousness (Schleiermacher) or his perfect vocation (Ritschl).
The two-natures doctrine uses outdated metaphysical categories.
(Some forms) Pre-existence and virgin birth are symbolic expressions of Jesus' significance.
positions/christology-from-below/origin: Friedrich Schleiermacher (The Christian Faith, 1821–22, rev. 1830–31), Albrecht Ritschl and the Ritschlian school, Adolf von Harnack; in the 20th century varied ‘from below’ approaches (Pannenberg's methodology, though orthodox in conclusion; John Hick's The Myth of God Incarnate, 1977).
positions/christology-from-below/stronge: It engages modern historical consciousness and the quest for the historical Jesus.
It begins where the first disciples began: with a man they met.
It makes Christ's humanity central and existentially accessible.
It cannot reach a truly divine Christ; it ends with a highly God-conscious man (adoptionism under another name).
Barth: it substitutes religious experience for revelation.
The New Testament's earliest documents (Paul's letters, Philippians 2) already contain high Christology, undermining the evolutionary picture.
positions/christology-from-below/respons: Advocates answer that the confession of divinity grows out of encounter with the human Jesus, as in the Gospels.
Pannenberg argued that a ‘from below’ method, through the resurrection, arrives at full Chalcedonian conclusions.
positions/christology-from-below/consequ: Dominant in 19th-century liberal Protestantism; provoked Barth's neo-orthodoxy and fundamentalist reaction.
Shaped the historical-Jesus quests (Schweitzer, 1906; ‘New Quest’ from 1953; Jesus Seminar 1985).
positions/impeccability/oneLine: Christ not only did not sin but could not sin, because the person acting in his human nature is the eternal Son, who cannot will evil; his temptations were nevertheless real.
positions/impeccability/coreClaims/0: The subject of Christ's acts is the divine Word; a divine person cannot sin.
positions/impeccability/coreClaims/1: Christ's human will was perfectly and freely united to the divine (Constantinople III).
positions/impeccability/coreClaims/2: Temptation can be real without the possibility of yielding — like an attack on an impregnable fortress.
positions/impeccability/coreClaims/3: Christ's victory is assured, guaranteeing salvation.
positions/impeccability/origin: Common patristic and medieval teaching (Augustine, John of Damascus, Aquinas, ST III q. 15); defended by Reformed theologians such as W. G. T. Shedd (1888) and in most Catholic and Orthodox theology.
positions/impeccability/strongestArgumen: If Christ could have sinned, God himself could have sinned — impossible (James 1:13).
God's plan of salvation would have been at risk.
It follows from the hypostatic union as defined at Chalcedon and Constantinople III.
positions/impeccability/strongestObjecti: If Christ could not sin, his temptations were not like ours and he is not a real example (Hebrews 2:18; 4:15).
A will that cannot choose otherwise seems not free in the libertarian sense.
It seems to make the human nature a passive instrument.
positions/impeccability/responses/0: Impeccabilists argue that real temptation is measured by intensity, not by the possibility of yielding — only one who never yields feels its full force.
positions/impeccability/responses/1: Freedom in its highest form is the inability to sin (Augustine's non posse peccare for the blessed).
positions/impeccability/consequences/0: Supports assurance in Christ's finished work.
positions/impeccability/consequences/1: Central in 19th–20th-century evangelical debates with peccabilists (Charles Hodge held a peccabilist view).
positions/peccability/name: Peccability (Christ could have sinned but did not)
positions/peccability/altNames/1: Fallen-nature Christology (Irving, Barth, T. F. Torrance — related)
positions/peccability/oneLine: Christ was genuinely able to sin, yet by his free obedience in dependence on the Spirit he did not; this makes his temptations and victory fully real.
positions/peccability/coreClaims/0: Genuine temptation implies a genuine possibility of yielding.
positions/peccability/coreClaims/1: Christ's sinlessness was achieved by moral struggle and reliance on the Spirit and the Word.
positions/peccability/coreClaims/2: (Irving, Barth, Torrance — a related but distinct claim) The Son assumed fallen human nature, sanctifying it from within, without himself sinning.
positions/peccability/origin: Suggested by some Antiochene theologians (Theodore of Mopsuestia); sharpened by Edward Irving in London (1820s), who was deposed by the Presbytery of Annan in 1833 for teaching Christ's ‘sinful flesh’; held by Charles Hodge (Systematic Theology, 1872) and many modern evangelicals; fallen-nature Christology taken up by Karl Barth and T. F. Torrance.
positions/peccability/strongestArguments: Hebrews says Christ was tempted ‘in all points like as we are’ and ‘learned obedience by the things which he suffered’.
Christ's real moral victory is the basis of his sympathy and example.
Gregory's principle (‘the unassumed is unhealed’) implies he took our actual, fallen condition.
positions/peccability/strongestObjection: It implies the possibility that a divine person could sin — impossible for God.
It threatens the certainty of salvation.
Assuming ‘fallen’ flesh seems to make Christ himself a sinner in need of redemption (the charge against Irving).
positions/peccability/responses/0: Peccabilists distinguish the hypothetical possibility of sin (in his human nature) from its moral certainty given his perfect will.
positions/peccability/responses/1: Irving, Barth and Torrance distinguish assuming fallen nature from committing sin: Christ sanctified our nature by perfect obedience.
positions/peccability/consequences/0: Irving's deposition contributed to the founding of the Catholic Apostolic Church.
positions/peccability/consequences/1: A live topic in contemporary evangelical and Reformed Christology.
positions/seven-sacraments/oneLine: Christ instituted seven sacraments (baptism, confirmation/chrismation, Eucharist, penance, anointing of the sick, holy orders and matrimony), efficacious signs that confer the grace they signify.
positions/seven-sacraments/coreClaims/0: Sacraments are visible signs instituted by Christ that truly confer grace ex opere operato (by the rite itself) when received without obstacle.
positions/seven-sacraments/coreClaims/1: There are exactly seven, accompanying the whole of life: initiation (baptism, confirmation, Eucharist), healing (penance, anointing) and service of communion (orders, matrimony).
positions/seven-sacraments/coreClaims/2: Baptism, confirmation and orders imprint an indelible "character" and are not repeated.
positions/seven-sacraments/coreClaims/3: Sacraments are entrusted to the Church and normally require a validly ordained minister (except baptism and, in the West, marriage).
positions/seven-sacraments/origin: The early Church used "mystery"/"sacrament" broadly for many holy rites. Hugh of St Victor counted around thirty; Peter Lombard’s Sentences (c.1150) fixed seven. The number was professed at the Second Council of Lyon (1274), taught to the Armenians at Florence (1439) and defined by Trent (Session 7, 1547). The Orthodox commonly count seven mysteries since the 13th century (Confession of Peter Mogila, 1640) but treat the number less rigidly; the Church of the East’s lists (e.g. Abdisho of Nisibis, 1298) include the holy leaven and sign of the cross.
positions/seven-sacraments/proponentsOth: Abdisho bar Brikha (East Syriac variant list)
positions/seven-sacraments/strongestArgu: Each of the seven has a biblical basis in Christ’s or the apostles’ practice, and all were practised by the early Church.
East and West reached the same number independently enough that it reflects shared apostolic tradition, not a single school.
It expresses a fully sacramental view of creation and grace accompanying every stage of human life.
positions/seven-sacraments/strongestObje: Protestants argue that only baptism and the Supper have an explicit command of Christ joined to a visible sign and a promise of grace (Luther, Babylonian Captivity, 1520).
The number seven was not fixed until the 12th century, showing it is a later systematisation.
Critics argue that ex opere operato risks mechanical religion and clerical control of grace.
positions/seven-sacraments/responses/0: Catholics and Orthodox reply that the Church’s recognition of sacraments developed like the canon of Scripture, articulating what had always been practised.
positions/seven-sacraments/responses/1: Ex opere operato means Christ, not the minister’s merit, acts in the sacrament; fruitful reception still requires faith and disposition (Trent Session 7, canons 6–8).
positions/seven-sacraments/consequences/: Structured medieval and modern Catholic and Orthodox religious life (confession, last rites, sacramental marriage law).
A sharp point of division with Protestantism from 1520 onward.
Shapes Catholic canon law (e.g. marriage tribunals, annulments).
